newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt sees conference as showcase for reforms.
newsitem.headline: Egypt sees conference as showcase for reforms.

text.p: For Egypt, a favourite with international financiers seeking high returns in new markets, next week's Middle East and North Africa economic conference is a golden opportunity which it almost let pass.

But after a couple of weeks humming and hawing about the whys and wherefores of holding such a conference under the shadow of a right-wing government in Israel, President Hosni Mubarak decided that Egypt's bread was buttered on the side of showing the country off to hundreds of foreign businessmen.
"This conference is not being held for Israel," Mubarak said last month in explanation of his decision.

"We have asked all the world's major companies to attend and see development in Egypt. Perhaps they will take part in some of our activities to reinforce investment and increase production so people here may find more jobs," he added.

Ever since the previous such meeting in Amman last year, Egypt had given the Cairo meeting this year a special place in its timetable for accelerated economic liberalisation and integration into international markets.
U.S. Vice President Al Gore set the tone back in January, just after Mubarak shuffled his cabinet and told new Prime Minister Kamal Ganzouri to start moving on the economic front.

"I'm particularly excited about the 10 months between now and the economic summit," Gore said. "It is potentially the most exciting period of market opening, economic reform and rising living standards that Egypt has ever seen. We stand ready...to work closely to maximise the potential for this period of dynamic and dramatic change."
Hyperbole aside, the past 10 months have indeed seen more change than the previous three years of economic reform.
The government's accelerated privatisation programme has been the star of the show, winning plaudits from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Western governments.

In May, for the first time, the state relinquished majority control of a public-sector company through a flotation on the stock exchange. "It's a historic day for the whole Egyptian economy and in the modern history of Egypt," brokerage executive Ali el-Tahri said at the time.

The privatisation was a decisive factor in the IMF's decision to approve a new stand-by credit agreement with Egypt in October, clearing the way for the Paris Club to write off loans to Egypt worth about $4 billion.
Between April and September this year, $400 million in portfolio investments flowed into the Egyptian stock exchange from abroad, pushing the index up to 18-month highs.

In July, for the first time in decades, shares in an Egyptian company, Commercial International Bank, went on sale internationally through a global depositary receipt (GDR). Other such issues are expected to follow.
The government also eventually bit the bullet on trade liberalisation, pushing through surreptitiously the biggest cuts in import tariffs for more than two years.

And in a symbol of its desire to catch up with neighbours like Israel and Jordan, the government rushed into place a GSM mobile telephone network. Timed for the opening of the conference next Tuesday, it starts working on Thursday.
But at least one important target has fallen by the wayside -- a partnership agreement with the European Union.

Differences over the quotas for Egypt's agricultural exports to Europe have held up the negotiations and despite some last-minute activity the phased free trade agreement cannot possibly be ready by next week.
Taking their cue from Mubarak, Egyptian officials have been balancing the regional integration aspect of the conference with an emphasis on the potential benefits for their own country.

"Peace means that international investors can come and invest not only in regional projects but also in national projects in individual countries," said assistant foreign minister Raouf Saad, one of the key organisers.

But some foreign economists say they believe that Egypt will have trouble turning it into a business meeting for businessmen, isolating it from the antagonism between Arabs and the Israeli government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"The conference will bring Egypt up on the radar screens of companies that might not have noticed it," said a senior executive of an international bank.
"These high financiers are certainly going to rub shoulders but they won't be concluding any deals here," added a European economic diplomat based in Cairo.
"Let's be realistic. The show is highly political and because of the political tensions you won't be able to say it was a great success," he added.
